chapter: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
title: How Rhythm Town was written and why it never found a producer
summary: Spikes wrote the script from his war song The Fuehrer's Men Is Getting Fewer, producers visited rehearsals, an Erlanger interest faded, and the strike ruined the Beaux Arts run.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: You started writing lyrics very early. When was the first time you started writing screenplays and stories and things?

Well, I think when I wrote "Rhythm Town," you know. How come is...Clarence...it was in the newspaper that Clarence was going to get up a show so Austin and I had wrote a lot of songs, and I went over to see Clarence and say, "Well, if you..." It's during the war, and I wrote a big song called, "The Fuehrer's Men Is Getting Fewer Every Day." You know. And I went over to see Clarence, and the producers was there, and we played the song and I say...I say, "This is timely 'cause the name of it is 'The Fuehrer's Men Is Getting Fewer Every Day'." You know, the Fuehrer was losin' his men. Hitler was. And so he said, "Yeah." He...they didn't have no book or anything, so Clarence come over and say, "What have you got? You got a story or anything?" "No, what do you want?

I'll write one." And so, I started to writin' it, and we got four...five big producers and all the...Clarence brought a lot of people there from the studio. Even Mickey Rooney was over there, I think.

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Benjamin "Reb" Spikes
Conducted by Patricia Willard
Cassette 6
Okay, you were saying Mickey Rooney and...

Oh, I said they used...every week, they...they'd be four, five people come down and listen to rehearsal, you know, and they all liked the show and everything but they...they uh...we just didn't happen to find any. Lewis...at the Erlanger--he liked it very much but just as we...we give a try-out of our show down at the old Mayan one night, and they...he was told about it, and he was...wanted the show. I got a letters from him in there, but he went back East and stayed three or four months, and when he come back, we weren't together, you know. And so we never did get anywhere with it. So...three or four of us put in three or four hundred dollars apiece, and we went over and got the Beaux Arts, and that we thought it was going... And very after we got our money up and everything, the streetcar strikes, and the strike was three or four weeks. The theaters all downtown closed, and 'course, we had to pay three weeks guaranty to the Actors' Union, and by the time the three weeks was up, we didn't have no mon...enough money to move the scenery away from there. Yeah.
